dimension: Rating and ranking systems that produce an ordering from pairwise outcomes (Elo, Glicko, TrueSkill, Bradley-Terry/Plackett-Luce, tournament design, sample-efficiency and lock-in literature)
citations_that_failed: MISATTRIBUTED THEOREM — Tang, Wang and Jin, arXiv:2502.10985. The dimension says 'Theorem 2 and the surrounding analysis PROVE that under ARBITRARY matchmaking Elo can give inconsistent rankings even on strongly-stochastically-transitive instances'. Theorem 2 states the OPPOSITE-DIRECTION POSITIVE result: 'Under uniform matchmaking, theta^mle gives identical ranking as P-bar', with the formal version (Theorem G.1) holding when q_ij = q_i q_j (product matchmaking). The inconsistency result is EXAMPLE 1 — one specific 5-player SST matrix with one specific matchmaking distribution Q, theta^mle = [5.48, 0.89, 4.60, 0.04, 0], bootstrap intervals at T = 10000. The paper proves an existence counterexample, not a statement about arbitrary matchmaking. This is the most serious defect found: the dimension's SECOND DISAGREEMENT (the self-confirming leaderboard, which it calls 'more dangerous because it survives switching to Swiss') is sold as a theorem and is a numerical counterexample. The CONCLUSION still stands, because the Bolsinova et al. 2022 result independently establishes the adaptive-selection defect, but the evidentiary weight must be moved off 'Theorem 2'.

UNVERIFIABLE FIGURES — Klinkenberg, Straatemeier and van der Maas 2011. Citation itself CONFIRMED (Computers and Education 57(2):1813-1824, DOI 10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.003), and the 0.75 mean success probability CONFIRMED. But '3648 children' and '10 months' trace only to a later citing paper (Aas and Leithe) that describes Klinkenberg's work, not to the 2011 article; and '3.5 million arithmetic problems' could not be located in any source. Pelanek 2016 (local copy, Computers and Education, DOI 10.1016/j.compedu.2016.03.017), which surveys Elo in adaptive educational systems and cites Klinkenberg 6 times, gives Math Garden's scale as 'more than 100,000 students, who answered in total more than 15 million questions' — a different figure entirely. Under `measured-rate-travels-with-its-script`, these 3 numbers are claims about evidence, not evidence.

MISAPPLIED DOMAIN — Medo and Wakeling, arXiv:1001.3745. Citation CONFIRMED (EPL 91(4):48004, August 2010) and the quoted phrase about 'a significant impact on algorithms' performance' is accurate. But the paper is about ONLINE USER REPUTATION systems rating objects on discrete star scales, not about pairwise skill rating, and its second headline finding is that at low rating resolution INCREASED NOISE CAN IMPROVE overall system performance. The dimension uses it to support 'Discretisation loses information' for chess-style leagues; the paper neither studies that object nor points unambiguously in that direction.

QUOTE NOT VERBATIM, WRONG AUTHORITY — TrueSkill tau. The dimension writes that 'the reference documentation describes [tau] in his own words as \"the factor that restrains a fixation of rating\"'. The actual text is 'The dynamic factor which restrains a fixation of rating', and its source is the third-party Python `trueskill` package documentation (trueskill.readthedocs.io, Heungsub Lee), not Microsoft's TrueSkill reference. Double quotes signal verbatim under the project's quote convention; this is a close paraphrase, and 'the reference documentation' overstates the source's standing.

QUOTE NOT VERBATIM + MECHANISM CONFLATION — Milvang on the 2024 FIDE 1400 floor. The chess.com rendering is 'A rating floor [of] 1400 [divides] the players into rated and unrated players' — 'divides' is the reporter's bracketed edit, so the dimension's double-quoted 'divides the players into rated and unrated players' is not Milvang's verbatim wording. Worse, FIDE's 1400 is a LIST-INCLUSION THRESHOLD (fall below it and you drop off the rating list), whereas USCF floors at 100 and 1400 through 2100 are ANTI-DECLINE floors that stop a rating falling. The dimension cites them in one breath as evidence of the same lock-in mechanism. They are opposite devices.

PLAYER-COUNT ERROR — David (1959), Glenn (1960), Searls (1963). The dimension says all 3 'computed exact winning probabilities for 8 players'. Its actual source, Devriesere and Csato's tournament-design survey (local copy, line 446), says in prose 'Although limited to tournaments with 8 players, the authors find SKO to be the least effective format' — so the dimension reproduced the survey faithfully. But the SAME survey's Table 1b gives David (1959) n = 3-8 with worst format 'NS' (not specified), and Glenn (1960) n = 4 with worst format SKO. So Glenn is 4 players, not 8, and David's paper is not recorded as naming SKO worst. The dimension also cites all 3 as primary without disclosing that the survey is the actual source read.

PRIORITY OMISSION — Ford (1957), American Mathematical Monthly 64(8):28-33. The strong-connectivity iff-unique-finite-MLE result is CONFIRMED in substance, and the dimension's partition wording matches the literature's almost exactly. But Zermelo (1929) is standardly credited with the prior proof that the iteration converges to the unique MLE; the Bradley-Terry survey literature says the model was 'independently proposed by Zermelo (1929) and Ford (1957)'. Low severity, but a 1957-only attribution for a 1929 theorem is the kind of thing a referee flags.
quantitative_errors: FALSE PRECISION ON AN ORDER BOUND — 'For 700 models that is 699 comparisons against a floor of roughly 4600 — short by a factor of about 6.6, and the shortfall is information-theoretic, not an implementation detail.' The Negahban/Oh/Shah necessity sentence is CONFIRMED VERBATIM from the paper (arXiv:1209.1688, extracted text lines 217-220): 'It should be noted that Omega(n log n) is a necessary number of (random) comparisons for any algorithm to even produce a consistent ranking with high probability since with fewer edges (comparisons) the resulting random graph will be disconnected with positive probability.' But Omega(.) carries an unspecified constant and an unspecified log base, so no numeric floor follows. I computed the alternatives: 700*ln(700) = 4586 (the dimension's choice, constant 1, natural log); 700*log2(700) = 6616; and the paper's OWN sufficient condition in its Theorem 4 is m > 12 n log n, which for n = 700 is 55,029. The quoted 'floor of roughly 4600' and 'factor of about 6.6' are therefore one arbitrary point in a range spanning an order of magnitude.

CATEGORY ERROR — the Omega(n log n) bound is for RANDOM comparisons and does not bind a designed bracket. The paper's own justification is the Erdos-Renyi connectivity threshold: below n log n edges a RANDOM graph is disconnected. A single-elimination bracket is not a random graph. I tested its undirected comparison graph at n = 2, 4, 8, 16, 64 and 512: it is a CONNECTED SPANNING TREE with exactly n-1 edges in every case. So the disconnection mechanism that makes the bound necessary never fires for a bracket. The bracket's actual defect is DIRECTED acyclicity, which the dimension already has correctly from Ford (1957). The INFORMATION BUDGET section is the wrong instrument pointed at the right conclusion, and should be dropped or re-derived.

COLD-START COST UNDERSTATED BY UP TO 25x, AND THE DIMENSION'S OWN FISHER ARGUMENT IS THE PROOF. 'He just has to pay for roughly 12 to 48 observations per model, not 1.' I re-ran Glickman's RD equations varying only the expected score E (which the committed script fixes at 0.5): E = 0.50 gives 12 games to RD <= 100 and 48 to RD <= 50 (reproducing the dimension exactly); E = 0.75 gives 15 and 64; E = 0.90 gives 32 and 133; E = 0.99 gives 283 and 1206. The 12-to-48 figure is a BEST CASE attainable only under the near-equal pairing the dimension recommends ELSEWHERE in the same document. It is quoted in the passage arguing the founder can drop the difficulty ladder and keep RANDOM pairing — under which a heterogeneous 700-model roster produces mostly lopsided matchups and the requirement rises by the same 2.78x-to-25.3x factor the dimension itself computed from p(1-p). Internal inconsistency, and it points the wrong way on the founder's binding constraint.

ROSTER SIZE NEVER MULTIPLIED THROUGH. 'Roughly 12 to 48 observations per model' at the stated roster of 700 is 8,400 to 33,600 paid observations as a floor, and 93,100 to 844,200 at E = 0.9 to 0.99. The dimension states the per-model figure and never the total, in a design whose stated hard constraint is cost.

THE SWISS IS NOT A 7-ROUND SWISS. Running the committed bt_connect_rate.py reproduces every headline number EXACTLY (knockout 0/500 at scales 2.0, 4.0 and 8.0; Swiss-7 65/500 at scale 4.0, 132/500 at 8.0, 5/500 at 2.0; Swiss-10 239/500). But the script's own output reports 55 and 53 matches where a true 7-round Swiss on 16 players is 56: the greedy no-rematch pairing leaves players unpaired in some rounds. The bias runs AGAINST Swiss, so the conclusion 'Swiss is far better but still unreliable' is conservative — but the quoted counts are for a degraded, non-FIDE pairing heuristic, not for a Swiss system.

'KEPT DIVERGING' IS SATURATION, NOT MEASURED DIVERGENCE. bt_knockout.py reproduces 1.599e+301 as claimed (dimension says 1.6e+301), but the iteration sequence is 1.010e+301 at 10 iterations, 1.524e+301 at 100, 1.593e+301 at 1000, 1.599e+301 at 10000 — i.e. it plateaus against the IEEE double ceiling near 1.8e+308 rather than growing without bound across those 4 decades. The theoretical claim (MLE undefined, MM iteration divergent) is correct and guaranteed by Ford; the numbers do not demonstrate ongoing divergence.

THE KNOCKOUT 0-OF-500 MEASUREMENT IS A TAUTOLOGY. A single-elimination win graph is acyclic by construction, so strong connectivity cannot hold, so 0 of 500 is the only possible outcome at any upset level. Presented under the heading THE MEASUREMENT alongside THE THEOREM, it reads as independent corroboration. It is not: it is the theorem re-executed. (The Swiss arm of the same script IS informative.)
overstated_verdicts: Glicko: 'DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE' is self-contradicted within its own transfers_to_cdsfl field, which records 'Glicko assumes a central authority computing one update per rating period over all results, which conflicts with the peer-to-peer requirement'. The brief names 'must work with no central coordinator' as a HARD constraint. A mechanism the dimension itself documents as violating a hard constraint cannot be DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE; the honest verdict is REQUIRES_ADAPTATION or PARTIALLY_APPLICABLE, with the rating-period batch structure named as the thing that must be replaced. Same objection applies to the Glicko-2 verdict, which inherits the batch structure and makes it worse by requiring a LARGER rating period (10 to 15 games per player, confirmed verbatim in glicko2.pdf, versus 5 to 10 for Glicko).

'What is NOT already invented: nothing in this literature rates capability and COST jointly.' REFUTED. RouteLLM (Ong et al., arXiv:2406.18665, published at ICLR 2025 as 'RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs from Preference Data') fits a Bradley-Terry router on Chatbot Arena pairwise preference data (roughly 80,000 battles plus roughly 120,000 augmented samples) explicitly to trade quality against cost, reporting over 2x cost reduction at matched quality and evaluating with 2 purpose-built cost-quality metrics (call-performance threshold and average performance gain recovered). FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia, Zou, 2023) is the cascade version of the same idea. This is exactly the capability-and-cost intersection, built on exactly the Bradley-Terry machinery this dimension surveys. An unqualified universal after surveying the classical rating literature is the failure shape named in `feedback_check_the_whole_set`.

ROSTER SIZE 1 TO 700 IS NEVER ADDRESSED AT THE LOW END. Every mechanism assessed produces an ordering from PAIRWISE outcomes. At roster size 1 there are no pairs and every mechanism returns the prior unchanged (1500 / 350 / 0.06 forever); at roster size 2 Ford's condition fails for any number of games in which one participant never loses, so the MLE is undefined no matter how much is spent. The hard constraint spans the degenerate region and the dimension's DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE verdicts are silent about it.

'Glickman and Jensen (2005) proved [restricting the pairing pool to near-equals] is information-optimal.' Overstated. The paper (CONFIRMED: Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 127:279-293) formulates pairing as Bayesian optimal design maximising expected Kullback-Leibler gain from prior to posterior, solved by a combinatorial perfect-matching algorithm. Near-equal pairing is an OBSERVED PROPERTY of the resulting optimal designs under their linear paired-comparison model — and the paper's own statement of it is joint, not marginal: pairs are favoured 'when they are expected to be close in ability, AND the amount of uncertainty is large' (abstract text, local copy line 295). They did not prove a theorem that near-equal pairing is optimal; they derived a criterion whose solutions tend that way. The distinction matters because the uncertainty half is what makes a wide-RD newcomer worth pairing against an unequal opponent — which is the case the founder's cold-start problem is actually about.

'Discrete leagues are pure overhead AS AN ESTIMATOR.' The supporting production examples (Ubisoft on TrueSkill, Riot on unpublished MMR, FIDE titles on continuous Elo) are reasonable, but the only measurement offered is Medo and Wakeling, which is about star-rating reputation systems and reports that noise can help at low resolution. The claim is probably right and is currently unmeasured in its own domain.

missed_mechanisms.name: HodgeRank (combinatorial Hodge decomposition of a pairwise comparison graph)
missed_mechanisms.citation: Jiang, X., Lim, L.-H., Yao, Y. and Ye, Y., 'Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory', Mathematical Programming 127(1):203-244, 2011. NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED IN THIS SESSION — the web-search budget was exhausted before I could check it, so treat the volume and page numbers as unconfirmed.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: It is the one mechanism in this literature that answers BOTH of the constraints the dimension concludes are unmet. It solves a least-squares problem on the comparison graph rather than running a sequential central update, so it needs no rating period and no central authority with a global view — any party holding the edge set can compute it, and the computation is a graph Laplacian solve that distributes. And its Hodge decomposition splits the observed disagreement into a gradient (consistent, rankable) part plus LOCAL and GLOBAL CYCLIC parts, which is a direct numerical measure of how much of the roster's behaviour is genuine intransitivity. That is exactly the diagnostic the dimension needs and does not have: it diagnoses the knockout's acyclicity problem from Ford's theorem, and it diagnoses the routing-distortion problem from Bolsinova, but it offers no instrument that MEASURES either on live CDSFL data. HodgeRank is that instrument, and it works on incomplete and badly unbalanced graphs, which is what cost-constrained routing produces.

missed_mechanisms.name: Rank Centrality's own spectral estimator (not just its lower bound)
missed_mechanisms.citation: Negahban, S., Oh, S. and Shah, D., 'Rank Centrality: Ranking from Pairwise Comparisons', Operations Research 65(1):266-287, 2017, DOI 10.1287/opre.2016.1534. Verified from the full text (arXiv:1209.1688): Theorem 1 is stated for 'n objects and a CONNECTED comparison graph G', with sample complexity O(xi^-2 n poly(log n)) where xi is the spectral gap of the graph Laplacian.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension mines this paper for a lower bound and then misapplies it, while discarding the estimator — which is the better fit for its own stated gap. Rank Centrality is the stationary distribution of a random walk on the comparison graph, computed by POWER ITERATION: a local, repeatable neighbour-averaging step requiring no central authority, no rating period and no ordering of results. It needs only that the graph be connected (1 comparison per edge suffices; the n-1 edges of even a bracket give connectivity, as I verified at n = 2 to 512), and its error bound degrades gracefully through the explicit spectral-gap term xi, which gives CDSFL a computable number for how much a cost-skewed pairing pattern is costing it. Against the hard constraint 'no central coordinator', the dimension recommends Glicko — which it admits violates that constraint — while the paper it already read contains the estimator that does not.

missed_mechanisms.name: Cost-aware routing built on Bradley-Terry (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT)
missed_mechanisms.citation: Ong, I. et al., 'RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs from Preference Data', arXiv:2406.18665, June 2024; ICLR 2025. Chen, L., Zaharia, M. and Zou, J., 'FrugalGPT', 2023.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: It falsifies the dimension's single most consequential negative claim. 'Nothing in this literature rates capability and COST jointly' is the sentence that tells the founder the capability-plus-cost objective is novel territory where he must build. RouteLLM is a Bradley-Terry model fitted to Arena pairwise preference data and used to route under a cost constraint, with published cost-quality metrics and a reported 2x-plus cost reduction at matched quality — it is the intersection, already built, already measured, and already evaluated for transfer when the candidate models are swapped at test time. CDSFL should be compared against it as a baseline rather than told the ground is empty.

notes:
WHAT SURVIVES, AND IT IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART. No citation is fabricated. All 23 checked resolve to real work, and the 2 theorems the dimension's strongest disagreement actually rests on are confirmed close to verbatim. Vu and Shoham 2011 / Arlegi and Dimitrov 2020, from the Devriesere and Csato survey, line 468: "Balanced knockout tournaments with eight or more players cannot satisfy simultaneously that a) stronger players are favored over weaker players; and b) equally strong players are treated equally" — the dimension reproduced this exactly, including the 8-player threshold. Ford 1957's strong-connectivity iff unique finite MLE is confirmed in substance with the partition wording intact. Marchand 2002 is confirmed down to the issue and page range (JRSS-D 51(2):169-178, April 2002) and its conclusion is characterised correctly. Sziklai, Biro and Csato 2022 is confirmed (Computers and Operations Research 144:105821, n = 32, best format Swiss, worst SKO, at equal game count).

Both committed simulations reproduce EXACTLY on re-execution: bt_connect_rate.py returns knockout 0/500 at every scale, Swiss-7 at 65/500, 132/500 and 5/500 for scales 4.0, 8.0 and 2.0, and Swiss-10 at 239/500; bt_knockout.py returns 1.599e+301. The Glicko RD trajectory reproduces at 247, 143, 12 games to RD under 100, 48 to under 50, 135 to under 30. The Fisher-information arithmetic reproduces (SymPy argmax at 1/2, value 1/4; 0.09 at p = 0.9 for a 2.78x loss; 0.0099 at p = 0.99 for 25.25x). Ebtekar and Liu's Table 2 Codeforces row matches to the decimal including the column labels (Codeforces 78.3, TopCoder 78.5, TrueSkill 61.7, Elo-MM-chi 78.5, Elo-MMR 78.6) and the dataset line (1087 contests, 2999 average participants). Tang et al.'s Table 2 LLM Arena row matches to 4 decimals (0.6607, 0.6602, 0.6611, 0.6611, 0.6619), and Theorem 1's bound is exactly as quoted, (3/2)GD*sqrt(T) at step size eta_t = D/(G*sqrt(t)), with the per-round C*sqrt(N/T) at eta_t = sqrt(N/t). Every Glicko and Glicko-2 parameter claim checks verbatim against Glickman's own PDFs: 1500/350, the 350 cap, tau reasonable between 0.3 and 1.2 and as low as 0.2, volatility 0.06 "this value depends on the particular application", "The opponents' volatilities are not relevant", 5-to-10 games for Glicko against 10-to-15 for Glicko-2.

SO THE CORRECTIONS ARE REAL BUT NONE OF THEM REVERSES THE RECOMMENDATION. The knockout is still disqualified — by Ford, not by the information budget. Adaptive routing still distorts ratings — by Bolsinova et al. 2022 (citation confirmed: JRSS-C 71(1):91-118, DOI 10.1111/rssc.12523, authors correct, and the "no correction in Glicko, TrueSkill or TrueSkill 2" claim is corroborated by the same authors' 2022 follow-up in the British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, whose abstract states Urnings "accounts for adaptive item selection which, if not corrected for, may distort the ratings"), not by Tang et al.'s Theorem 2. Score groups still beat persistent leagues. The founder is still right about the cold start and about round 1.

TWO BOUNDARIES ON THIS REVIEW. First, the computed task text I was given is TRUNCATED mid-sentence inside the third mechanism entry ("If a model's capability jumps 10"), so I saw 3 mechanisms out of an unknown total and the closing part of the Glicko-2 transfer assessment. My missed-mechanism findings are deliberately restricted to items absent from BOTH the visible prose AND the source documents the dimension demonstrably fetched into the scratchpad — which include the Devriesere and Csato tournament survey, Ebtekar and Liu, Glickman and Jensen's adaptive paired comparison design, Beygelzimer, Langford and Ravikumar's Error-Correcting Tournaments, Karnin, Koren and Somekh's sequential halving, Yan et al.'s dueling-bandits top-Elo paper, Cseh et al.'s Swiss Gambit, Pelanek's Elo-in-education survey, Balkir et al. on adaptive LLM evaluation, and a routing-oracle preprint. Dueling bandits, sequential halving, error-correcting tournaments and KL-optimal adaptive pairing are therefore probably covered in the part I could not see, and I have not reported them as misses. Second, the web-search budget for this turn was exhausted at 200 calls before I could verify the HodgeRank reference or Glickman's 2001 Journal of Applied Statistics 28:673-689 volume and page numbers; both are flagged as unconfirmed rather than asserted.

ONE STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION THAT IS NOT A CITATION DEFECT. The dimension diagnoses the routing-distortion problem and then recommends Glicko, which it quotes Bolsinova et al. as containing no correction for that exact problem, while Urnings — the one system it names as correcting for it — is listed only under "what is NOT already invented". If the adaptive-selection defect is the dangerous finding, and it is, then Urnings deserves a mechanism entry and a verdict of its own rather than a mention in the negative-space paragraph.
